extracted.intended_audience: researchers and academics interested in peer review and reproducibility (ecologists, journal editors, reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how consistent/preventable pre-publication peer-review decisions are (e.g., via resubmission experiments) and what factors affect that reproducibility. The page comments on a classic experiment and suggests follow-up tests across journal types and samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility of pre-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether peer-review and editorial decisions are consistent when the same work is re-submitted (the page title and text refer to the 'reproducibility of peer review').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on Peters & Ceci (1982): twelve psychology papers were resubmitted with fake author names/affiliations 18–32 months after original publication; only three of the twelve were detected as duplicates and eight of the remaining nine were rejected. The post notes this implies low reproducibility, but cautions the dataset is small and from a different field, so results may not generalize to ecology. Suggests replicating the experiment in other fields and journal types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of duplicate submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether journals/editors detect that a resubmitted manuscript is a duplicate of a previously published paper (phrased in the post as 'detected as duplicates').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the referenced study only 3 of 12 were detected as duplicates. This is an implicit quality metric for editorial screening procedures (plagiarism/duplication checks). The blog implies such detection rates reflect on reproducibility and editorial controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for rejection: methodological flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of methodological rigor as grounds for rejecting manuscripts (the post: 'rejected, in many cases on grounds of serious methodological flaws').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiment's resubmitted papers were often rejected citing serious methodological flaws, which suggests reviewers invoke methodological criteria. The author notes this pattern is troubling because it calls into question whether focusing review on 'technical soundness' would improve reproducibility. Implies methodological assessment is central but may be applied inconsistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of peer review: 'technical soundness' vs broader criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether limiting peer review to assessing only 'technical soundness' (as some journals like PLOS ONE do) would affect the reproducibility of decisions (the post: 'limiting pre-publication peer review to considering “technical soundness” would not actually increase the reproducibility').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that the rejection reasons in Peters & Ceci suggest that constraining reviewers to technical soundness alone might not make outcomes more reproducible. The post encourages testing this hypothesis empirically (e.g., comparing PLOS ONE-style review to selective journals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal selectivity/type effects on reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: How journal editorial policy and selectivity (selective journals vs soundness-focused journals like PLOS ONE) influence consistency of review outcomes (the post: 'It would be good to also try it with Plos One as well as with selective journals').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests that reproducibility might differ by journal type; recommends comparative experiments across journal classes to assess the role of selectivity and scope in review variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling considerations: accepted vs rejected papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of the sample of manuscripts used to measure reproducibility (the post: 'And to try it with rejected papers as well as accepted papers... obtaining a random sample of rejected papers would be tricky').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that including only accepted (or only published) papers biases measurement of reproducibility; measuring across both accepted and rejected manuscripts is important but poses logistical challenges. Sampling strategy is thus a methodological criterion for studies of review reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of resubmission experiments to quantify randomness in review
rubrics_metrics.description: Conducting controlled resubmission experiments (resubmit previously published papers with altered authorship/affiliations) to quantify randomness in pre-publication peer review (the post references Peters & Ceci and 'other approaches to quantifying the randomness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests such experiments are feasible ('It wouldn’t be that hard…') and recommends trying them in ecology and across journal types. Practical notes: need to consider ethical and logistical issues, time lag between original and resubmission, and difficulty getting random samples of rejected work.
